summary: OO modelling = find **objects** (nouns become classes and attributes) and their **behaviour** (verbs become responsibilities and methods) in the requirements, then model how they interact.

The modelling steps, in order: identify classes (entity / boundary / control), add attributes and methods, add relationships, add multiplicities, then sequence diagrams for behaviour and interaction, enhance class details (discover more methods), implement, test.
Short example: Professor mentors 1..* Students, Student registers 1..* Courses, Result holds the grade. A sequence diagram per scenario then reveals the methods each class needs.
Blackjack case study: list nouns, eliminate (synonyms, plurals, attributes, the system itself), list verbs as responsibilities, review them, write CRC cards, then draw the UML class diagram.
Final blackjack classes: **Card, Deck, Hand, Dealer, Player**. Bet was kept in the noun review but dropped at the responsibility review ('can be added later').
mustMemorise: Entity = persistent information tracked by the system (icon: circle sitting on a line).
Boundary = interaction between actor and system (icon: circle with a T-bar on its left).
Control = logic to realise a use case (icon: circle with an arrowhead on top).

Steps: Identify classes, then attributes & methods, then relationships, then multiplicities, then behaviours & interaction (functional flow), then enhance class details, then implement, then quality testing.
Nouns become candidate classes or attributes. Verbs become responsibilities (methods).
CRC = Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators. Card fields: Class Name, Superclasses, Subclasses, Responsibilities, Collaborators.
CRC cards were introduced by Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham (OOPSLA '89, 'A Laboratory for Teaching Object-Oriented Thinking').
Why CRC: portable (no computer), participants experience the system first-hand by role-playing objects, good for teaching the OO paradigm.

Eliminated nouns: Blackjack (game = the system), House (synonym for dealer), Players (one Player class suffices), Cards (one Card class), Face value & Suit (attributes of Card), Ace/King/Queen/Jack (attributes of Card).
Deck composed of 52 Cards (filled diamond at Deck). Each Player and the Dealer has a Hand.

items.title: Modelling real-world systems
notes: The primary goal of OO: model real-world systems **in ways similar to how people think**.
Identify objects (encapsulated data and behaviour) by finding **nouns and verbs** in the requirements statement.

items.title: Steps 1-4 and entity / boundary / control
notes: Steps in order: **Identify classes, then add attributes and methods, then add class relationships, then add multiplicities**.
**Entity** (circle on a line) = persistent information tracked by the system, e.g. Student, Course.
**Boundary** (circle with a T-bar on its left) = interaction between actor and system, e.g. a form or a device interface.
**Control** (circle with an arrow on top) = logic to realise a use case, e.g. `AppMgr`, `UserMgr`.

items.title: Steps 5-8
notes: Then: **identify object behaviours and interaction through functional flow** (sequence diagrams), **enhance class details** (this is where you *discover more methods*), **implement the model**, **quality testing**.
Trap: behaviour modelling comes **after** the first class diagram, and it feeds new methods back into the classes.

items.title: Short example: class diagram from nouns
notes: The underlined nouns became classes: Professor, Student, Course, Result. All are **entities** (circle-on-line icon).
Professor `1` to Student `1..*` with roles `mentor`/`mentee`: a professor mentors **at least 1** student, and each student has exactly **1** mentor. Multiplicity is read at the far end.

Student `1..*` to Course `1..*` (`register`). Student to Result is `1..*`. Result to Course is a solid line with an **open arrowhead** = navigable **association** (Result knows its Course). It is not a dependency, which would be dashed.
The note `as Student Record` is attached by a **dashed line** (a comment, not a relationship). Result has private attributes `-grade`, `-semYr`.

items.title: Only model what the requirement needs
notes: Same diagram, but `semYr` has been **removed** from Result. The highlighted requirement (check course results) only needs `grade`.
Lesson: attributes come from the requirement text, not from guessing.

items.title: sd check mentee result
notes: Professor (actor) sends `select` to `:SelectForm` (boundary), which sends `showMenteeResults()` to `AppMgr` (control), which calls the entities. This is the actor, boundary, control, entity layering.
`getMentees()` goes to the professor. Then `loop [foreach student]` calls `getResults()`, with a nested `loop [foreach result]` calling `getCourse()`, `getCourseName()`, `getGrade()`.
All calls have filled heads (synchronous). `output` is a **dashed** return back to SelectForm.
The dashed lines drawn inside the loop boxes are not meaningful: a loop has a single operand. They come from the drawing tool.

items.title: 'x N': sequence diagrams add methods to classes
notes: Repeat (**x N**) a sequence diagram per scenario. Each message received becomes a **method on the receiver's class**: `getResults()` on Student, `getCourse()` and `getGrade()` on Result, `getCourseName()` on Course.
Mismatch: the sd sends `getMentees()` to Professor, but the class box lists `+getMenteeResults()`. If asked, the rule is that the method name must match the message.
Attributes added: `-name` (Professor, Student) and `-courseName` (Course). `-` = private, `+` = public.

items.title: Blackjack requirements: nouns circled
notes: Nouns are circled in the requirements statement (game, dealer, house, players, cards, deck, face value, hand, card, aces, Jack/Queen/King, bet, draw). They are the raw material for classes.
Source of the case study: *The Object-Oriented Thought Process* (Matt Weisfeld), named on slide 11.

items.title: Blackjack class diagram
notes: Deck to Card: **filled diamond at Deck**, `52` at Card = **composition** (a deck is made of 52 cards). The diamond sits at the whole.
Player `1` to Hand `1` and Dealer `1` to Hand `1` (`show`). Dealer `1` to Player `1..*` (`give card`). Dealer to Deck (`deals`).
The small filled triangles next to `show` / `give card` / `deals` show the **reading direction of the association name**. They are not inheritance and not navigability.

Notation quirks: `+getValue:int` omits `()` (standard UML is `+getValue(): int`). `Player:` / `Deck:` are the constructors. Members with no symbol (`limit:int`, `startNewGame:void`, `random:Random`) have unspecified visibility. `-determineWinner: Player` is private.

items.title: 'Goal of game' is oversimplified
notes: The slide says the winner's value 'will be equal to 21'. The actual rule (slides 12 and 23) is **closest to 21 without exceeding it**. Over 21 loses.
If a question asks about the rules, use slide 23: closer to 21 than the dealer wins.

items.title: Dealer's role (verbs)
notes: Dealer: deals cards, gives extra cards on request, shows all or part of a hand, calculates the hand value, calculates the number of cards, determines the winner and starts a new hand.
These verbs later become Dealer responsibilities (slides 41, 48).

items.title: Card & Deck requirement
notes: A card knows and reports its **face value**. **Suit is of no importance**.
Every card belongs to a deck. There are **52 cards in a deck**. The deck must deal the next card and report how many cards remain. This is the basis of composition with multiplicity 52.

items.title: Card values
notes: Suits are no factor. **Ace = 1 or 11**. **Jack, Queen, King = 10**. Other cards = their face value.

items.title: Win / payout rules
notes: Closer to 21 than the dealer wins an amount **equal to the bet**. Winning with a **blackjack pays 3:2**. **Over 21 is not a win**.
Draw (slide 24): identical scores **and at least 17**, and the player keeps the bet.

items.title: Case-study design steps (overview)
notes: Order used in the case study: **study the requirements again**, then **identify classes** (list nouns, then eliminate), then **identify responsibilities** (list verbs, then review), then **CRC cards**, then **UML class diagram**.
Slide 27: expect the first CRC cards to change, because not every class you think of makes the final cut.

items.title: The noun list
notes: Game, Blackjack, Dealer, House, Players, Player, Cards, Card, Deck, Hand, Face value, Suit, Winner, Ace, Face card, King, Queen, Jack, Game, Bet. 'Game' appears twice on the slide.

items.title: Process of elimination (struck-out nouns)
notes: Struck out: Blackjack, House, Cards, Face value and Suit (both 'an attribute of Card'), Winner, Ace, Face card, King, Queen, Jack, Bet.
The red strike line is drawn on **Player**, but slide 32 says **Players** is eliminated and Player is kept. Player is a final class, so answer **Players eliminated**.
Kept: Game, Dealer, Player, Card, Deck, Hand ('cards on hand'). Game is never drawn as a class. Per slide 32, the game is the system itself.

items.title: Why Blackjack, House, Players were removed
notes: **Blackjack**: eliminated because the **game is the system itself**.
**House**: just **another name for the dealer** (a synonym).
**Players**: one **Player class** suffices (do not model plurals as classes).

items.title: Why Cards, Face value, Suit were removed
notes: **Cards**: a single Card class is enough.
**Face value** is an **attribute** of Card.

**Suit**: not needed for blackjack (you might keep it for future card games). 'Our example will leave it out', yet the final UML (slides 13, 60) still has `-suit:String` with `getSuit`/`setSuit`. The slides are inconsistent here.

items.title: Ace, King, Queen, Jack become attributes
notes: They are better represented as **attributes of Card**, not as individual classes (no subclass per rank).

items.title: Bet: in, then out again
notes: Here: Bet was originally removed but is **kept** 'because of future card usage', so it appears on slide 36's picture.
Slide 50 later: the Bet class is **not needed** and 'can be added later if necessary'. The final design has no Bet.

items.title: Candidate classes after elimination
notes: Card, Deck, Hand, Dealer, Player, Bet. (Bet is dropped at slide 50, leaving **5 final classes**.)

items.title: Responsibilities come from verbs
notes: **Responsibilities relate to actions**: look for **verbs** to find each class's responsibilities. Nouns give classes, verbs give responsibilities.

items.title: Deck and Hand responsibilities
notes: Deck: shuffle, deal next card, know how many. Hand (slide 40): know how many cards, know the value, show the hand.
Slide 46 adds a Deck responsibility: **know whether there is a full deck to begin**.

items.title: Reviewing Card responsibilities
notes: Card: face value, suit. 'Face card / ace / joker?' does **not** need separate responsibilities, because **report value** handles it.

items.title: Review: renames for Dealer and Player
notes: Dealer: 'Calculate the value of the dealer's hand' is renamed **'Show the value of dealer's hand'**.
Player (slide 49): 'Calculate the value of the hand' is renamed **'Show value of the player's hand'**. Calculation belongs to Hand (Hand knows its value).

items.title: Bet class dropped
notes: Bet responsibilities: type of bet, value of bet, how much the player has left, whether the bet can be covered.
Decision: **'This class is not needed at this site, and can be added later if necessary.'**

items.title: CRC card fields
notes: CRC cards are used to identify objects and the messages they exchange.
Fields: **Class Name, Superclasses, Subclasses, Responsibilities (left column), Collaborators (right column)**.
CRC = **Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators**. Collaborators = the other classes this class works with or sends messages to.

items.title: History of CRC cards
notes: Introduced by **Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham** in *'A Laboratory for Teaching Object-Oriented Thinking'* (1989). The original purpose was **teaching programmers the OO paradigm**.
Beck changed 'Collaborators' to 'helpers'. Cunningham changed it back.
Typo: the slide says 'OOPLSA '89'. The conference is **OOPSLA** '89. Do not confuse with Ch9 originators (OCP = Bertrand Meyer, LSP = Barbara Liskov).

items.title: Why use CRC cards
notes: 1) **Portable**: no computers needed. 2) Participants **experience first-hand** how the system works by physically **playing the role of an object**. 3) Useful for **teaching the OO paradigm**.

items.title: Card and Deck CRC cards
notes: **Card**: responsibilities Get name, Get value. Collaborator **Deck**.
**Deck** (slide 56): Reset deck, Get deck size, Get next card, Shuffle deck, Show deck. Collaborators **Dealer, Card**.

items.title: Dealer, Player, Hand CRC cards
notes: **Dealer**: Start a new game, Get a card. Collaborators **Hand, Player, Deck**.
**Player** (slide 58): Want more cards?, Get a card, Show hand, Get value of hand. Collaborators **Hand, Dealer**.
**Hand** (slide 59): Return value, Add a card, Show hand. Collaborators **Player, Dealer**.
Each CRC responsibility maps to a method in the UML: e.g. Want more cards? is `+moreCards:boolean`, Add a card is `+addToHand`, Get next card is `+getNextCard:Card`.

items.title: Blackjack UML (final class diagram)
notes: The slide's text (partly hidden behind the picture in this render): UML shows a class with its attributes and methods. **`+` = public, `-` = private**.
Hand: `-value:Int`, `-hand:Vector`. Deck: `-cards`, `-shuffledCards`, `-nextItem`, private helpers `-createHearts/Spades/Clubs/Diamonds`, public `+shuffleDeck`, `+getNextCard:Card`, etc.
No Bet class. Card still has `-suit:String` despite slide 33. The same notation quirks as slide 13 apply (no `()` on methods; some members have no visibility symbol).

items.title: Design is iterative
notes: The design is not final: teams discuss, and **changes do take place**, but the CRC cards plus the class diagram are a start for writing the code.
